header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

# How this program reports what it found

This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.

The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.

## This file and the skills

When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.

This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".

## What a department delivers

Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:

- `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
- `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.

Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.

## The evidence rule

A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.

Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.

## The finding

```json
{
  "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
  "cwe": "CWE-798",
  "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
  "severity": "high",
  "confidence": "confirmed",
  "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
  "file": "config/env/all.js",
  "line": 8,
  "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
  "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
  "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
  "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
  "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
}
```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
| `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
| `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
| `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
| `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
| `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
| `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
| `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
| `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
| `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
| `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
| `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
| `fix` | what to change. |
| `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |

## Checking your own work before you commit

```sh
node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
```

That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.

## What the integration delivers

The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.

`findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:

```sh
for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
```

Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.

`SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

<deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>

- critical: 0
- high: 0
- medium: 0
- low: 0
- info: 0

## Executive summary

<the same in English>

- critical: 0
- high: 0
- medium: 0
- low: 0
- info: 0

## Scope and method

<the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>

## Findings

### critical

- `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>

### high

...

## What was not covered

- <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
- <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>

## Certificate

Verified findings: <count>
Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>

<one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
```

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>

"line": 48,
"snippet": "app.post(\"/profile\", isLoggedIn, profileHandler.handleProfileUpdate);",

"evidence": "server.js:7 `// const csrf = require('csurf');` and server.js:104-113 (the whole `app.use(csrf())` block and the res.locals.csrftoken helper) are commented out, so no CSRF middleware runs anywhere in the app despite `csurf` being a listed dependency in package.json:11. 1: # access — authentication, session handling and authorization
2: 
3: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). Read-only; nothing was written into the target tree.
4: 
5: ## Method
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` printed `1.177.0`, so semgrep ran: `semgrep --config /home/user/deepseek-harness/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/semgrep --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat`. It scanned 72 git-tracked files with 113 rules and returned 29 hits. Every hit was treated as a place to read, not as a finding. The access-relevant hits were the `express-cookie-settings` family on `server.js:78` (no-httponly, no-secure, no-expires, no-domain, no-path, default-name) and the hardcoded-secret hit on `config/env/all.js:8`; both were read in full (server.js:1-157, config/env/all.js) before deciding what to report. The `express-open-redirect` hit on `app/routes/index.js:72` and the `eval`/injection hits in `app/routes/contributions.js` are outside this department's scope (injection/platform) and are not reported here.
8: 
9: Beyond the scanner, every route registration was read in `app/routes/index.js` and the target.json manifest, and for each one the middleware chain in front of it was traced into `app/routes/session.js` (the only source of `isLoggedIn`/`isAdmin` middleware), then the handler and its DAO were read end to end: `app/routes/{session,profile,allocations,benefits,contributions,memos,research,tutorial}.js` and `app/data/{user,profile,allocations,benefits}-dao.js`, plus `server.js`, `config/config.js`, `config/env/all.js`, and `package.json` (to confirm `csurf` and `helmet` are dependencies but never invoked in `server.js`).
10: 
11: ## Route table (what was actually registered, in `app/routes/index.js`)
12: 
13: | Method | Path | Middleware chain | Handler |
14: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
15: | GET | `/` | none | displayWelcomePage |
16: | GET/POST | `/login` | none | displayLoginPage / handleLoginRequest |
17: | GET/POST | `/signup` | none | displaySignupPage / handleSignup |
18: | GET | `/logout` | none | displayLogoutPage |
19: | GET | `/dashboard` | isLoggedIn | displayWelcomePage |
20: | GET/POST | `/profile` | isLoggedIn | displayProfile / handleProfileUpdate |
21: | GET/POST | `/contributions` | isLoggedIn | displayContributions / handleContributionsUpdate |
22: | GET/POST | `/benefits` | isLoggedIn | displayBenefits / updateBenefits |
23: | GET | `/allocations/:userId` | isLoggedIn | displayAllocations |
24: | GET/POST | `/memos` | isLoggedIn | displayMemos / addMemos |
25: | GET | `/learn` | isLoggedIn | inline redirect handler |
26: | GET | `/research` | isLoggedIn | displayResearch |
27: | * | `/tutorial/*` | none (mounted router) | tutorial pages, static content only |
28: 
29: `isAdmin` (`sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware`, `app/routes/session.js:25-34`) is built at `app/routes/index.js:27` but is never placed in any route's middleware chain — grep over the file confirms the only two uses of the identifier are its declaration and this unused assignment. Every route above that reaches a database read or write does so with, at most, "is some user logged in", never "is this the right user" or "is this user an admin".
30: 
31: ## Findings
32: 
33: Six findings, all `confirmed` (the full path from route registration through middleware to handler to DAO/query was read for each):
34: 
35: 1. **`access-001-idor-allocations`** (`app/routes/index.js:63`, CWE-639, high) — `/allocations/:userId` trusts the path parameter with only an is-logged-in check; the DAO queries by that raw id with no ownership predicate, and ids are small sequential integers, so any authenticated user can enumerate other users' allocation data.
36: 2. **`access-002-benefits-missing-admin-check`** (`app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862, high) — `POST /benefits` has an `isAdmin` middleware sitting unused right next to it; without it, any authenticated non-admin user can rewrite any other user's `benefitStartDate` by posting an arbitrary `userId`.
37: 3. **`access-003-session-fixation-login`** (`app/routes/session.js:116`, CWE-384, medium) — login sets `req.session.userId` without regenerating the session id first; the fix is described in a comment directly above the line and is even implemented a few lines later for signup, but not for login.
38: 4. **`access-004-csrf-missing-on-state-changing-routes`** (`app/routes/index.js:48`, CWE-352, medium) — `csurf` is a declared dependency but its `app.use(csrf())` is commented out in `server.js`, so none of the six state-changing POST routes carry a CSRF token or an Origin check.
39: 5. **`access-005-non-constant-time-password-compare`** (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`, CWE-208, low) — login compares passwords with `===` rather than a constant-time/hash verify; the bcrypt-based fix is present in a comment but not on the live code path.
40: 6. **`access-006-session-no-absolute-expiry`** (`server.js:78`, CWE-613, low) — the `express-session` cookie configuration has no `maxAge` and no `secure` flag (the whole `cookie` block is commented out), so a session id, once issued, has no absolute server-side expiration.
41: 
42: Full detail, evidence and fixes for each are in `findings/access.json`.
43: 
44: ## What was not covered
45: 
46: - **Injection, XSS, SSRF, ReDoS**: `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34` (`eval()` on request input), `app/routes/research.js:14-16` (SSRF via `req.query.url`), `app/routes/index.js:72` (open redirect via `req.query.url`), and the NoSQL `$where` construction in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73-79` were read enough to see they exist but are outside this department's brief (injection/data) and are not scored here.
47: - **Secrets**: the hardcoded `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` in `config/env/all.js:8-9` (and the matching `development.js`/`test.js` files) were seen via semgrep and are a `secrets`-department finding, not reported here beyond this note.
48: - **Headers/platform**: `helmet` is a dependency but every `app.use(helmet.*)` call in `server.js:38-65` is commented out; this is noted for context but scored as `platform`, not `access`.
49: - **Signup/mass-assignment for `isAdmin`**: read `app/data/user-dao.js:addUser` and `app/data/profile-dao.js:updateUser` specifically looking for a route where a caller can set their own `isAdmin`/role field; neither `handleSignup` nor `handleProfileUpdate` reads or forwards an `isAdmin`/role field from `req.body`, so no self-privilege-escalation route of that shape was found — this was checked, not skipped.
50: - **Runtime behavior**: no request was ever sent to a running instance; everything above is a static read. Whether a reverse proxy, WAF, or infrastructure-level control in front of a real deployment narrows any of this was not checked and could not be from source alone.
51: - **MFA**: NodeGoat has no MFA/OTP code path at all in the routes read; there is nothing to evaluate for CWE-308 in this codebase.
52: - **Rate limiting / brute force**: confirmed by grep (`rate-limit|rateLimit|express-brute` — no matches anywhere in the tree) that no rate-limiting package is installed and no handwritten attempt counter exists around `handleLoginRequest`; this was read as a real gap but is folded into the CSRF/session findings above rather than issued as a separate line-cited finding, since there is no single line whose absence can be cited beyond the route registration already covered by finding 3.

(End of file - total 52 lines)
</content>

| GET | `/research` | isLoggedIn | displayResearch |
| * | `/tutorial/*` | none (mounted router) | tutorial pages, static content only |

`isAdmin` (`sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware`, `app/routes/session.js:25-34`) is built at `app/routes/index.js:27` but is never placed in any route's middleware chain — grep over the file confirms the only two uses of the identifier are its declaration and this unused assignment. Every route above that reaches a database read or write does so with, at most, "is some user logged in", never "is this the right user" or "is this user an admin".
## Findings
Six findings, all `confirmed` (the full path from route registration through middleware to handler to DAO/query was read for each):

1. **`access-001-idor-allocations`** (`app/routes/index.js:63`, CWE-639, high) — `/allocations/:userId` trusts the path parameter with only an is-logged-in check; the DAO queries by that raw id with no ownership predicate, and ids are small sequential integers, so any authenticated user can enumerate other users' allocation data.

2. **`access-002-benefits-missing-admin-check`** (`app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862, high) — `POST /benefits` has an `isAdmin` middleware sitting unused right next to it; without it, any authenticated non-admin user can rewrite any other user's `benefitStartDate` by posting an arbitrary `userId`.

3. **`access-003-session-fixation-login`** (`app/routes/session.js:116`, CWE-384, medium) — login sets `req.session.userId` without regenerating the session id first; the fix is described in a comment directly above the line and is even implemented a few lines later for signup, but not for login.

4. **`access-004-csrf-missing-on-state-changing-routes`** (`app/routes/index.js:48`, CWE-352, medium) — `csurf` is a declared dependency but its `app.use(csrf())` is commented out in `server.js`, so none of the six state-changing POST routes carry a CSRF token or an Origin check.

5. **`access-005-non-constant-time-password-compare`** (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`, CWE-208, low) — login compares passwords with `===` rather than a constant-time/hash verify; the bcrypt-based fix is present in a comment but not on the live code path.

6. **`access-006-session-no-absolute-expiry`** (`server.js:78`, CWE-613, low) — the `express-session` cookie configuration has no `maxAge` and no `secure` flag (the whole `cookie` block is commented out), so a session id, once issued, has no absolute server-side expiration.
Full detail, evidence and fixes for each are in `findings/access.json`.
## What was not covered

- **Injection, XSS, SSRF, ReDoS**: `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34` (`eval()` on request input), `app/routes/research.js:14-16` (SSRF via `req.query.url`), `app/routes/index.js:72` (open redirect via `req.query.url`), and the NoSQL `$where` construction in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73-79` were read enough to see they exist but are outside this department's brief (injection/data) and are not scored here.

- **Secrets**: the hardcoded `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` in `config/env/all.js:8-9` (and the matching `development.js`/`test.js` files) were seen via semgrep and are a `secrets`-department finding, not reported here beyond this note.
- **Headers/platform**: `helmet` is a dependency but every `app.use(helmet.*)` call in `server.js:38-65` is commented out; this is noted for context but scored as `platform`, not `access`.

- **Signup/mass-assignment for `isAdmin`**: read `app/data/user-dao.js:addUser` and `app/data/profile-dao.js:updateUser` specifically looking for a route where a caller can set their own `isAdmin`/role field; neither `handleSignup` nor `handleProfileUpdate` reads or forwards an `isAdmin`/role field from `req.body`, so no self-privilege-escalation route of that shape was found — this was checked, not skipped.

- **Runtime behavior**: no request was ever sent to a running instance; everything above is a static read. Whether a reverse proxy, WAF, or infrastructure-level control in front of a real deployment narrows any of this was not checked and could not be from source alone.
- **MFA**: NodeGoat has no MFA/OTP code path at all in the routes read; there is nothing to evaluate for CWE-308 in this codebase.

- **Rate limiting / brute force**: confirmed by grep (`rate-limit|rateLimit|express-brute` — no matches anywhere in the tree) that no rate-limiting package is installed and no handwritten attempt counter exists around `handleLoginRequest`; this was read as a real gap but is folded into the CSRF/session findings above rather than issued as a separate line-cited finding, since there is no single line whose absence can be cited beyond the route registration already covered by finding 3.

for this review; nothing was written into it.
This is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the
mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`).
1. **Manifest read first.** `package.json` was read in full (65 lines). It
declares 16 production dependencies (`dependencies`) and 20 development
dependencies (`devDependencies`), plus one tarball dependency
(`grunt-if`, pulled from a GitHub tarball URL rather than the registry —
noted, not separately scored). `package-lock.json` is present
(`lockfileVersion: 2`), so it is the authoritative, resolved version set
this review audits, not the caret/tilde ranges in `package.json`.
2. **`semgrep --version`** printed `1.177.0`, so semgrep ran. It was pointed
at the local rule pack only
(`/home/user/deepseek-harness/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/semgrep`);
the `p/owasp-top-ten` registry pack was not additionally fetched because
this review is scoped to dependencies, and semgrep's code-pattern rules do
not identify dependency advisories in any case. It found 8 hits, all
outside this department's scope (a Mongo-`$where` pattern in
`app/data/allocations-dao.js`, an `eval`-on-input pattern in
`app/routes/contributions.js`, and hard-coded-secret patterns in
`config/env/{all,development,test}.js`) — read as places to look, never
treated as dependency findings, and left for the injection/secrets
departments.
3. **`npm audit --json`** was run inside the target
(`cd /root/targets/NodeGoat && npm audit --json`). It reached the live npm
registry: the command exited 1 with a fully populated report (not a
network-error shape), so **the audit did not fail to reach the
registry** — this is a real, current advisory read, not a fallback.
`npm audit`'s own summary: **145 vulnerable packages** across the resolved
tree of 1,479 total packages (396 prod, 1,016 dev, 116 optional) — 38
critical, 66 high, 33 moderate, 8 low, 0 info.
4. Individual advisory chains were traced with a small Node script over the
audit JSON (walking `via`, distinguishing a package's own advisories from
the advisories of the transitive packages it depends on), and cross-checked
against `npm view <pkg>@<version> deprecated` / `time.modified` against the
live registry for maintenance status and current-latest-version staleness.
Resolved (lockfile) versions were read directly from
`package-lock.json`'s `packages` map, not assumed from the `package.json`
range.
5. Per the department's grouping rule, findings below are **one per direct
dependency**, each stating how many transitive advisories/packages it
carries, not one finding per transitive package the audit lists — 145
flagged packages collapse to 13 findings below, one per direct dependency
that actually pulls in an advisory or carries an explicit upstream
deprecation notice.

`package.json`. Of those, 16 production dependencies are listed in
`package.json`; **10 of the 16 production dependencies carry an advisory or
an explicit upstream deprecation notice** (`body-parser`, `csurf`, `express`,
`express-session`, `forever`, `helmet`, `marked`, `mongodb`, `swig`,
`underscore`), plus one more (`bcrypt-nodejs`) that carries no advisory but an
explicit "no longer maintained" notice on a security-sensitive package. The
remaining 6 production dependencies (`consolidate`, `dont-sniff-mimetype`,
`needle`, `node-esapi`, `serve-favicon`) were checked and carry **no** flagged
advisory in this audit; that is coverage of currently-known, disclosed issues
only, not a clean bill of health.

GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (arbitrary code execution, CWE-94) plus
GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (unbounded-recursion DoS). Fixed in `1.13.8`.
- **`swig` (`^1.4.2` → `1.4.2`, the only version ever published)** — critical,
own advisory GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (arbitrary local file read, CWE-22), with
`fixAvailable: false` because the npm registry itself marks the package "no
longer maintained." There is no version that fixes this; it has to be
replaced.
- **`mongodb` (`^2.1.18` → `2.2.36`)** — critical, own advisory
GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (DoS, CWE-400) plus a critical deserialization advisory
in bundled `bson` (GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr, CWE-502). The registry's own
deprecation notice on this line says "Please upgrade to 2.2.19 or higher";

22: middleware stack, in file order, from `require` to `listen`), then every file

24: table and the mounted error handler), `app/routes/error.js` and
25: `app/views/error-template.html` (the error path), `app/routes/session.js` and
26: `app/data/user-dao.js` (login, to check for rate limiting), `config/config.js`

29: `package.json` (dependency list, to confirm what security middleware is and
30: is not installed), and the client-side assets under `app/assets/js` and the
31: view templates that load `environmentalScripts` (checked for DOM/URL trust
32: issues and for whether debug tooling reaches production pages).

37: worked example of the fixes being written and then switched off: helmet is
38: required and configured, then the entire block is commented out (lines
39: 10, 39-65); the session cookie's `httpOnly`/`secure` block is written and
40: commented out (lines 92-100); the CSRF middleware is written and commented
41: out (lines 104-113, left to the access department since CSRF is its brief);
42: the HTTPS listener is written and commented out in favor of
43: `http.createServer` (lines 144-155); and swig's `autoescape` is explicitly
44: set to `false` (line 137). Every platform finding below either lives in this
45: file or is a direct consequence of a value it defines (`cookieSecret`,
46: `environmentalScripts`) being handled unsafely elsewhere.

48: - **No security headers** (`server.js:10`, CWE-693): helmet is never mounted
49:   anywhere in the file; the app ships the default `X-Powered-By`, no CSP, no
50:   frame protection, no HSTS.

52:   **missing `Secure`** (`server.js:78-102`, CWE-614): the `cookie` option is
53:   never passed to `express-session`, and the server never listens over TLS
54:   (`server.js:144-147`, CWE-319, cleartext transmission) — the session

103: - low: 1

108: - **CSRF** (`server.js:104-113`, csurf commented out) and session-fixation on
109:   the login path are real and were read, but CSRF, session management and
110:   authentication are explicitly the `access` department's brief; not filed

113:   `res.redirect(req.query.url)`) and the **`eval()` on user input** in

done 32733
### critical

- `dep-underscore-rce` — underscore resolves to a version with a critical arbitrary-code-execution advisory (`package.json:23`, CWE-94, confirmed) — underscore ships in the production dependency tree (package.json 'dependencies', not devDependencies). An attacker who can influence input into underscore's template compiler can execute arbitrary code in the Node process serving the whole application; deeply nested or circular input into _.isEqual/_.flatten can crash the process. Fix: Bump the declared range to "^1.13.8" (the first published version clear of both advisory ranges) and regenerate package-lock.json.
- `dep-swig-file-read` — swig template engine has an unpatched arbitrary local file read advisory and is abandoned upstream (`package.json:22`, CWE-22, confirmed) — swig is the view-rendering engine wired through `consolidate` for NodeGoat's HTML templates; a template-rendering path that reaches this advisory lets an attacker read arbitrary files off the server filesystem, and because the package is abandoned there is no upgrade path that removes the bug short of replacing the engine. Fix: Migrate off swig to a maintained engine reachable through the same `consolidate` abstraction (e.g. Nunjucks or EJS); no version bump within the swig package fixes this.
- `dep-mongodb-driver-outdated` — mongodb driver is 5+ major versions behind, with its own DoS advisory and a critical deserialization advisory in bundled bson (`package.json:18`, CWE-400, confirmed) — mongodb is the application's database driver (used throughout app/data/*-dao.js). A malformed BSON document reaching the deserializer, or a crafted request that triggers the driver's own DoS path, can crash the process or corrupt in-memory state for every request being served. Fix: Upgrade the mongodb driver; at minimum move past 3.1.13 to clear the driver's own advisory, but given the API and dependency changes accumulated since 2.x, plan the upgrade to a current 6.x/7.x release and update app/data/*-dao.js call sites for the new driver API.
- `dep-forever-prototype-pollution-chain` — forever, the process supervisor Procfile starts the app with, carries a critical prototype-pollution chain (`package.json:15`, CWE-1321, likely) — If forever's config-loading path (nconf) or its argument parsing (optimist/minimist) ever parses attacker-influenced input, prototype pollution in the process that supervises and restarts the whole application is a critical-blast-radius bug: it can affect every request handled after pollution occurs. Fix: Upgrade forever to 4.0.3 (a semver-major bump, per `npm audit`'s own `fixAvailable` suggestion), which drops the vulnerable flatiron/nconf/optimist chain; re-verify the Procfile invocation still works with the new major's CLI.
- `inj-eval-pretax` — Server-side code injection via eval() on the contributions pre-tax field (`app/routes/contributions.js:32`, CWE-95, confirmed) — An authenticated user can submit a payload such as `require('child_process').execSync('id')` (or any JS expression) as the preTax form field; it executes in the Node.js server process with full access to the process, filesystem and network, giving full remote code execution. Fix: Replace eval(req.body.preTax) with Number(req.body.preTax) or parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10), then validate the parsed number as the existing isNaN/range checks already attempt to do.
- `inj-eval-aftertax` — Server-side code injection via eval() on the contributions after-tax field (`app/routes/contributions.js:33`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Same as the preTax sink: an authenticated user can supply arbitrary JavaScript in the afterTax field and have it executed server-side, yielding remote code execution. Fix: Replace eval(req.body.afterTax) with Number(req.body.afterTax) or parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10) before the numeric validation.
- `inj-eval-roth` — Server-side code injection via eval() on the contributions roth field (`app/routes/contributions.js:34`, CWE-95, confirmed) — Same as the other two sinks: an authenticated user can supply arbitrary JavaScript in the roth field and have it executed server-side, yielding remote code execution. Fix: Replace eval(req.body.roth) with Number(req.body.roth) or parseInt(req.body.roth, 10) before the numeric validation.
- `inj-nosql-where-allocations` — NoSQL $where injection in the allocations threshold filter (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`, CWE-943, confirmed) — Any authenticated user can send e.g. `?threshold=0'; return true; var x='` or `?threshold=0';while(true){}` to make MongoDB evaluate attacker-supplied JavaScript inside its $where clause: this can bypass the intended filter to dump other users' allocation records, or hang the shared mongod process in an infinite loop, denying the database to every other user of the application. Fix: Never build $where from request input. Parse threshold with parseInt and validate it is within an expected numeric range (0-99), then express the comparison as a normal query operator, e.g. { userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }, so MongoDB never executes attacker-controlled JavaScript.

If a deployment follows the tutorial's own instructions and uncomments the HTTPS block in server.js without replacing this key pair, an attacker who has cloned the repository can decrypt captured TLS traffic or impersonate the server in a man-in-the-middle attack against any client that trusts the certificate. Fix: Remove the committed key and certificate from the repository and its history, generate a fresh key pair per deployment (or via a CA/ACME), and load it only from a secret store or mounted volume, never from a path inside the source tree.
48: 
49: ### low
50: 
51: - `access-005-non-constant-time-password-compare` — Login compares passwords with a plain === instead of a constant-time or hash-verify comparison (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`, CWE-208, confirmed) — An attacker with low-latency network access to the login endpoint could, in principle, use response-time differences to narrow down a victim's password character by character faster than blind brute force, though this requires a very clean timing channel to be practical. Fix: Store passwords hashed with bcrypt (bcrypt.hashSync on signup) and verify with bcrypt.compareSync, which is constant-time with respect to the secret, instead of ===.
52: - `access-006-session-no-absolute-expiry` — Session cookie is configured with no maxAge/expiry and no Secure flag, so sessions never expire server-side (`server.js:78`, CWE-613, confirmed) — A session id, once obtained (e.g. via network capture, XSS, or a shared machine), remains valid indefinitely with no absolute expiration, extending the window an attacker can reuse a stolen session. Fix: Set an explicit cookie.maxAge (and re-issue/rotate the id periodically), and once the app serves over HTTPS, set cookie.secure: true so the session cookie is never sent in the clear.
53: - `dep-express-session-cookie-onheaders` — express-session bundles low-severity cookie and on-headers advisories (`package.json:14`, CWE-241, confirmed) — express-session issues the application's session cookie on every authenticated request; the bundled cookie/on-headers advisories allow malformed cookie attributes or header manipulation at the edges of what the library validates, which is low severity on its own but sits directly on the session-management path. Fix: Upgrade express-session to a current 1.19.x release so it pulls cookie >=0.7.0 and on-headers >=1.1.0.
54: - `dep-csurf-archived` — csurf is archived and no longer maintained upstream, and bundles a low-severity cookie advisory (`package.json:11`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — csurf is the CSRF-protection middleware in this app. It is not currently the target of an open CVE, but with the package archived, any future CSRF-bypass finding against it will never be patched upstream; the immediate cookie advisory is low severity. Fix: Plan a migration off csurf to a maintained CSRF library before relying on it long-term (the deprecation notice itself points to Express's own discussion board for current recommendations); in the meantime bump the resolved cookie dependency to >=0.7.0.
55: - `dep-bcrypt-nodejs-unmaintained` — bcrypt-nodejs, the password-hashing dependency, is explicitly deprecated with no active CVE found (`package.json:8`, CWE-1104, confirmed) — No known exploit exists in the code as read. The risk is that bcrypt-nodejs, being unmaintained, will not receive a fix if one is ever found in its hashing or salt-generation code, on a package that directly protects stored user passwords. Fix: Migrate to the actively maintained `bcrypt` (native binding) or `bcryptjs` (pure JS) package the deprecation notice itself recommends; verify the hash format is compatible or plan a rehash-on-login migration.
56: - `generalist-grunt-if-floating-git-tarball` — Build dependency is installed from a mutable GitHub branch tarball instead of a versioned, integrity-checked npm release (`package.json:51`, CWE-829, likely) — A compromise of the upstream branch (or a MITM without TLS pinning at install time) lets an attacker run arbitrary code in the build/CI environment the next time dependencies are installed, potentially exfiltrating CI secrets or poisoning the published artifact. Fix: Pin grunt-if to a specific commit SHA (e.g. `git+https://github.com/binarymist/grunt-if.git#<commit>`) or vendor/replace it with a registry-published, version-locked alternative, and verify the lockfile records that fixed reference.
57: - `platform-007` — Environment defaults to "development", which injects a live-reload debug script, unescaped, into every rendered page (`config/config.js:5`, CWE-489, confirmed) — A deployment that forgets to set NODE_ENV=production ships development tooling (and the unescaped-interpolation pattern it depends on) to real users, and signals to an attacker that verbose/dev behavior may be reachable elsewhere in the app. Fix: Fail closed instead of defaulting to "development" (e.g. require NODE_ENV to be set, or default to "production"), and never interpolate config-driven script tags without escaping.
58: - `secrets-zap-api-key-dev` — OWASP ZAP API key hard-coded in development and test configuration (`config/env/development.js:6`, CWE-798, confirmed) — Limited: this key only grants control of a local OWASP ZAP proxy instance used for the project's own security regression testing on a private IP; it does not grant access to the NodeGoat application or its data. Anyone who can already reach that private ZAP instance would not need this key to be meaningfully more dangerous, but the key is still committed in cleartext and reused verbatim in config/env/test.js. Fix: Read the ZAP API key from an environment variable or local, gitignored file instead of committing it, even for development/test tooling.
59: - `secrets-zap-api-key-test` — OWASP ZAP API key hard-coded again in the test environment configuration (`config/env/test.js:6`, CWE-798, confirmed) — Same as the development.js instance: limited to controlling a local ZAP proxy instance on a private network used for this project's own security scans. Fix: Read the ZAP API key from an environment variable or gitignored local file in both development.js and test.js rather than duplicating the literal.
60: - `secrets-crypto-key-dead-code` — Hard-coded AES key shipped in config for a currently-disabled encryption feature (`config/env/all.js:9`, CWE-321, possible) — No impact today, because the encryption path that would use this key is disabled (dead code). If a developer follows the tutorial's own suggested fix and uncomments profile-dao.js without first replacing cryptoKey, this exact hard-coded key would become the key used to encrypt SSNs, dates of birth and bank account/routing numbers for every user, and anyone with the repository would be able to decrypt that data. Fix: If the encryption feature in profile-dao.js is ever enabled, generate cryptoKey from an environment-provided secret or a KMS-managed key rather than this literal, and rotate/remove the literal from config/env/all.js regardless.
